plants.name: Bottlegourd

care.label: Sow indoors
care.value: late Apr to early May, in 4-in pots (4-5 wks before transplant)

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: ~60-80 days from sow to tender edible gourd (120+ if left to mature/dry)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 2-3 ft apart, 1-2 plants on the arch

care.label: Water
care.value: Heavy and consistent in Jul-Aug fruiting (vine is thirsty); deep drip 2-3x/week, taper as nights cool in Sep.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Yes: seed germinates best in warm ~80-85F soil and the hard seed coat can rot in cool soil, so the heat mat is the most reliable way to start it here.

plants.tip: Hand-pollinate in the evening: bottlegourd opens white flowers at dusk and our daytime bee traffic misses them, so transfer pollen from male to female flowers by hand to get fruit set in a short cool season.

plants.name: Ridgegourd

care.label: Harvest
care.value: late Aug to Sep (marginal; often no usable fruit)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 18-24 in apart at base of arch

care.label: Water
care.value: Heavy consistent water through warm season via drip; never let dry while flowering/fruiting; taper in Oct.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Essential: seeds need 85-90F soil to germinate and rot at cool PNW indoor temps without bottom heat.

plants.tip: Pre-soak seeds 24h, start on heat mat, and pre-warm soil with black plastic for 2 weeks before transplant; even then Sammamish's 75-80F summer rarely gives enough heat units for reliable ridge gourd, so treat it as an experimental crop and hand-pollinate female flowers in the morning to maximize the few fruit you get.

plants.name: Bitter gourd
plants.variety: Seeds of India (generic Indian karela type)

care.label: Harvest
care.value: late Aug to early Oct (light, weather-dependent)

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 60-75 days from transplant (often longer/marginal in cool summers)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 18-24 in apart at base of arch, single vine trained up trellis

care.label: Water
care.value: Consistent drip through warm season; keep evenly moist Jul-Sep, never let dry during fruit set. Taper in Oct.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Heat mat is mandatory: karela needs 80-90F soil to germinate and will rot in cool PNW potting mix without bottom heat.

traits: Hard seed coat - soak/nick before sowing
Slowest gourd in PNW - marginal yield
plants.tip: Karela is the most marginal gourd here; maximize heat by holding seedlings indoors until soil is reliably >65F (early-mid Jun), give it the hottest front-yard spot against a south wall/arch, and hand-pollinate (transfer male to female flowers each morning) since cool dull mornings suppress bee activity and fruit set.

plants.name: Cucumber

care.label: Plant out
care.value: early to mid Jun, once nights stay above 50F (late May only under a cloche)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 12 in apart on trellis, single row

care.label: Water
care.value: Heavy, even water (1-2 in/wk) once fruiting; drip daily in dry Jul-Aug. Inconsistent water causes bitter, misshapen fruit.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Heat mat helps but is not essential: cucumber germinates from ~60F up, though warm media (70-85F) speeds it and avoids rot in cool PNW spring indoor temps.

plants.tip: Do not rush transplanting: wait until nights stay above 50F, which is early June in Sammamish. Cold-stunted cucumbers sulk all season and never recover vigor.

plants.name: Eggplant

care.label: Water
care.value: Steady, even moisture through summer via drip; deep 1-2x/wk in dry Jul-Aug. Avoid drought stress which drops blossoms; taper as nights cool in fall.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Yes, the heat mat is mandatory: eggplant germinates poorly below 75F, and bottom heat at 80-85F is the difference between a good stand and rotted seed in a cool March windowsill.

traits: Heat-loving / marginal in cool PNW summers
Needs black mulch or wall-o-water for heat
plants.tip: Eggplant is the most heat-demanding crop here and a real gamble in cool maritime summers; full sun in the front yard plus black plastic mulch and an early wall-o-water to bank soil heat is the only way Rhim Jhim ripens before fall chill stalls it. Cover with floating row cover at transplant to block flea beetles.

plants.name: Okra

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 50-60 days from transplant (in heat); often 70+ here

care.label: Water
care.value: Steady deep drip 1 in/wk through warm dry Jul-Aug; never let dry out while flowering. Taper in Sep.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Yes, mandatory; okra needs 80-90F soil to germinate and will rot in cool damp seed flats without bottom heat.

plants.tip: Maximize heat: transplant against a south wall or use black plastic mulch plus a clear cloche/low tunnel early to bank soil warmth, or yield will be minimal.

plants.name: Peppers
plants.variety: Bell (California Wonder 300), Italian Sweet, Jalapeno (Early), Hot Bhaji

care.label: Plant out
care.value: early to mid Jun, once nights stay above 50F (late May only under a wall-o-water or cloche)

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 65-75 days green to first fruit from transplant; 90+ for red/ripe

care.label: Water
care.value: Steady, even moisture via drip through summer (~1 in/week); avoid drought stress that causes blossom drop and bitter fruit. Taper in Oct.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Essential: pepper seed germinates slowly and erratically below 75F, so the heat mat at 80-85F soil temp is the difference between 7-day and 3-week germination.

plants.tip: In cool maritime summers peppers underperform without help: plant in the hottest front-yard spot, use black plastic/landscape fabric mulch to warm soil, and prioritize the small fast varieties (Jalapeno Early, Italian Sweet) over slow big bells, which may only ripen green.

plants.name: Tomatillo

care.label: Water
care.value: Consistent moisture in summer via drip (1-1.5 in/wk) during the dry Jul-Aug stretch; ease off as fall rains return.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Use the heat mat - tomatillos germinate best at 75-85F and our April-May indoor temps are too cool for reliable, fast sprouting.

plants.tip: One of the more dependable warm crops in Sammamish's cool summers: it sets fruit even with nights in the 50s. Plant at least 2 (they are self-incompatible, so a lone plant sets empty husks), cage them, and pick when the fruit fills and splits the papery husk, from August until the October rains.

plants.name: Roselle / Gongura

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: ~60 days to leaf harvest; 120+ for calyces (rarely reached here)

care.label: Water
care.value: Consistent moisture in summer via drip, 1-2x/week deep; tolerates dry Jul-Aug once established but grows lusher with steady water. Reduce in fall.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Yes, heat mat is essential; seeds need 75-85F soil to germinate reliably and our spring soils are far too cold.

plants.tip: Grow this for the tart Gongura leaves, not calyces: roselle only flowers as days shorten in fall, and nearby frost records go as early as October 1, with cold nights stalling it before then. Calyces rarely form here, so harvest leaves through summer. Cool nights keep growth slow and yields modest.

plants.name: Sunflowers
plants.variety: Mixed (likely a blend of branching multi-head types like Autumn Beauty/Velvet Queen and single-stem giants like Mammoth/Russian Giant)

care.label: Harvest
care.value: Aug to Oct (blooms); Sep-Oct for mature seed heads

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 70-95 days (flowering); +30-45 days more for dry seed heads

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 6 in for cut-flower density; 12-18 in for branching types; 18-24 in for giants

care.label: Water
care.value: Keep soil moist through germination and early growth; drip 1-2x/week deeply through dry Jul-Aug. Drought-tolerant once established but blooms bigger with steady water.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Skip the heat mat; sunflowers are direct-sown and germinate fast once soil hits 60F+ in late May/June, so indoor starting adds no value and risks transplant-shocking their taproot.

traits: Tall types need staking in wind
Succession-sow single-stem types every 2-3 wks; branching types rebloom on their own
plants.tip: Protect emerging seedlings from slugs (Sluggo/bait) the first 2 weeks—they are the only real threat in cool maritime springs; sunflowers thrive in your full-sun front border and reliably bloom by August.

plants.name: Basil

care.label: Water
care.value: Consistent moisture all summer; drip 2-3x/week in dry Jul-Aug, water at base to keep foliage dry and avoid downy mildew. Ease off as fall cools.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Use the heat mat; basil germinates poorly below 70F and the mat holds soil at 75-85F for fast, even sprouting.

plants.tip: Do not rush transplanting; wait until nights stay above 50F (mid-June here) or cold-shocked plants stall and blacken. Pinch tops weekly to delay flowering and keep leaves coming.

plants.name: Marigold

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 50-60 days to first bloom from sow

care.label: Water
care.value: Moderate, even moisture while establishing; drought-tolerant once set. Drip 1-2x/week summer, keep foliage dry to limit fungal issues.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Use the heat mat for indoor starts: marigold germinates best at 70-75F soil, which an unheated PNW windowsill won't hit in March.

plants.tip: Don't rush them outside; marigolds sulk and rot in cold wet soil, so wait until late May when soil tops 60F, then they bloom nonstop until first frost.

plants.name: Spinach

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: Spring: late Feb-early Apr; Fall: mid-Aug-early Sep; Overwinter: September

care.label: Harvest
care.value: Apr-Jun (spring), Oct-Nov, then Feb-Mar from overwintered

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 3-4 in apart, rows 8-12 in; thin seedlings to stand

care.label: Water
care.value: Keep soil consistently moist on drip spring/fall; dry spells trigger bolting. Minimal water for overwintering plants.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Skip the heat mat; spinach germinates best in cool 45-65F soil and direct sows outdoors, while warm soil suppresses germination.

plants.tip: Spinach bolts fast once June's long days arrive, so spring sowings stop in early April. The easier crops here are fall and winter: sow mid-August for October-November picking, then a September sowing that rides out winter small under a cloche and regrows for February-March. Pick off leaves with leaf-miner trails promptly.

plants.name: Arugula
plants.variety: Rocket Salad (Gourmet Greens) - standard salad/wild-type rocket

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: early Mar through late Apr (spring), then late Aug through late Sep (fall); skip hot Jul-early Aug

care.label: Harvest
care.value: mid-Apr through Jun, then Oct through Nov (add 1-2 wks for backyard shade)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 1 in apart in rows 4-6 in apart; thin to 2-3 in for full leaves, or broadcast for baby-leaf cut-and-come

care.label: Water
care.value: Keep evenly moist on drip; consistent water prevents bolting and bitterness. Increase frequency in dry Jul-Aug, light in cool spring/fall.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat needed; arugula germinates fine in cool soil (40-55F) and is direct-sown outdoors, so the mat offers no benefit.

plants.tip: Float a row cover over seedlings at sowing to block flea beetles, which shotgun-hole the leaves in this region; the partial shade also slows bolting, letting spring sowings run later than full sun.

plants.name: Lettuce

care.label: Sow indoors
care.value: early Mar - early Apr (optional for first flush)

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: mid Apr - late Aug (succession every 2-3 wks)

care.label: Harvest
care.value: late May - Oct (gaps in peak Jul-Aug heat)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 8-10 in apart for full heads; 2-4 in for cut-and-come-again

care.label: Water
care.value: Even, consistent moisture year-round; never let dry out or it turns bitter/bolts. Drip 2-3x/wk spring/fall, daily in dry Jul-Aug.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Skip the heat mat; lettuce germinates fine at room temp and goes dormant above ~80F soil, so cool starts are better.

plants.tip: The backyard partial shade is the asset here, it slows bolting through dry Jul-Aug, but slugs are the real threat here; ring seedlings with Sluggo (iron phosphate) at transplant and reapply after rain.

plants.name: Coriander / Cilantro

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: mid-Apr through Sep, succession every 2-3 wks

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 2-3 in apart, rows 6 in; thin lightly

care.label: Water
care.value: Steady moisture spring-fall; drip keeps soil evenly damp, which delays bolting. Never let it dry out in summer.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat needed; cilantro is direct-sown only (taproot resents transplant) and germinates fine in cool 50-65F maritime soil.

plants.tip: In Sammamish the partial-shade backyard is ideal: shade plus the cool maritime climate and a fall sowing (Aug-Sep) give the longest leaf harvest before bolting; spring sowings bolt fast once dry July heat arrives.

plants.name: Dill

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: late Apr to mid-Jul (succession every 3 wks)

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 40-50 days to leaf; 90+ to seed head

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 8-10 in apart, thin seedlings; rows 12 in

care.label: Water
care.value: Even, moderate moisture via drip through summer; dry soil triggers early bolting. Less water needed in shaded backyard.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Skip the heat mat; dill resents transplanting and is direct sown, and it germinates fine in the 60-70F soil of late spring.

plants.tip: Sow in succession every 3 weeks from late April through mid-July, since dill bolts fast; April sowings sprout slowly in our cool soil. Partial shade in the backyard slows bolting and extends the leaf harvest. Let one final plant flower to feed beneficial insects and self-sow.

plants.name: Sorrel

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: Mar-May (hardy; no need to wait for frost to pass)

care.label: Harvest
care.value: May through Oct (mild spells into winter)

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 50-60 days from sow; light cutting sooner

care.label: Water
care.value: Even moisture spring-fall keeps leaves tender; drip 1-2x/week, more in dry Jul-Aug. Drought makes leaves tough and bitter.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Skip the mat; sorrel germinates at cool room temps and can go outside in early spring.

traits: Bolts in heat - pinch flower stalks
plants.tip: Red-veined sorrel is a hardy perennial here: it comes back every spring in the backyard bed and keeps leafing through our mild falls, often into winter. Cut flower stalks as soon as they appear to keep leaves tender; part shade slows bolting. Divide the clump every 3-4 years in spring.

plants.name: Carrot

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: late Apr - mid Jul (succession every 3 wks)

care.label: Harvest
care.value: Jul - Nov (storage roots from fall sowings)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 2 in apart, rows 6 in; 1/4-1/2 in deep

care.label: Water
care.value: Keep top 1 in constantly moist for 2-3 wks until germination; then steady drip 1 in/wk. Even moisture prevents splitting; avoid drought-then-soak.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat: carrots are direct-sown only, and the mat is irrelevant for outdoor germination.

traits: Needs constant surface moisture to germinate
Carrot rust fly - use row cover
plants.tip: Two things decide carrots here. Germination: keep the seeded row damp under a board or burlap until sprouts show (10-21 days), then remove it. Carrot rust fly: it has three generations a year in Washington and the fall one does the most damage, so lay fine row cover the day you sow, seal the edges, and keep it on. Lift fall carrots by late November instead of leaving them in all winter. Your raised beds suit long Nantes roots; no rocks to fork them.

plants.name: Beet

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: early Apr to late Jul (succession every 3 wks)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 3-4 in apart after thinning, rows 10-12 in

care.label: Water
care.value: Consistent 1 in/wk via drip spring-fall; even moisture prevents woody, cracked roots and bolting. Less in cool wet shoulders.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat needed; beets are direct-sown outdoors and germinate fine in cool 50-65F maritime soil.

traits: Each seed is a cluster - thin to 1 seedling
plants.tip: Each "seed" is a multi-seed cluster, so thin ruthlessly to one seedling per spot at 2-3 in tall (eat the thinnings as baby greens) or roots will stay marble-sized. Beets thrive in the 4-5 hr dappled backyard.

plants.name: Radish

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: mid-Mar to early May, then late Aug to mid-Sep

care.label: Harvest
care.value: late Apr through Jun, and late Sep through early Nov (allow ~1-2 wks extra for shade/cool)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 1 in apart, rows 4-6 in; thin promptly

care.label: Water
care.value: Even, consistent moisture is critical; drip daily in dry Jul-Aug heat to prevent cracking and pithy/hot roots. Steady spring/fall moisture otherwise.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat; radishes are direct-sown and germinate readily in cool 45-75F soil, so the mat is unnecessary.

traits: Thin promptly or roots won't form
plants.tip: Float row cover over seedlings from sowing until harvest to block flea beetles and cabbage root maggot fly; skip the heat of Jul-Aug (roots turn pithy and bolt) and resume succession sowing in late summer for a fall crop.

plants.name: Kohlrabi

care.label: Sow indoors
care.value: late Feb - mid Mar (spring); not needed for fall

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: early May - mid Jul (best as Jul-Aug fall crop)

care.label: Harvest
care.value: Jun-Jul (spring) and Sep-Oct (fall), +1-2 wks slower in shade

care.label: Water
care.value: Even, consistent moisture via drip; dry spells cause woody, cracked bulbs. Steady water Jul-Aug critical.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Use the heat mat for early indoor starts in Feb-Mar to get reliable germination while soil is cold; not needed for summer/fall direct sowing.

traits: Needs steady water or bulbs turn woody
Harvest at tennis-ball size before bulbs split
plants.tip: Harvest Konan at 2-3 in (tennis-ball size); leaving it longer in shade gives woody, pithy bulbs. A summer-sown fall crop is the most reliable here.

plants.name: Bunching onion / scallion

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 1/2 in apart, rows 4-6 in; no thinning needed

care.label: Water
care.value: Even moisture spring-fall; shallow roots dislike drying out. Drip 2-3x/wk in dry Jul-Aug, minimal in winter.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat needed; scallions are direct-sown outdoors and germinate fine in cool maritime soil without bottom heat.

plants.tip: Scallions are among the easiest year-round crops here. Sow every 3-4 weeks from mid-April to mid-July for summer and fall picking, and an August sowing overwinters for spring. The first April sowing is slow to sprout in cold soil (2-3 weeks). Cut stalks 1 in above the soil and they regrow.

plants.name: Garlic
plants.variety: Hardneck (German Red, Chesnok Red) — best for PNW; softneck Inchelium Red keeps longer

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: plant cloves mid-Oct to early Nov, 2-3 in deep, pointed tip up, 6 in apart

care.label: Harvest
care.value: July (cut scapes in June; dig bulbs when the bottom 2-3 leaves brown)

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: ~240 days from fall planting to midsummer bulbs

care.label: Water
care.value: Winter rain is enough; water regularly Mar-Jun as bulbs swell (drip 2-3x/wk), then stop in late June so skins dry down before the July harvest.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat — garlic is grown from cloves planted directly in the soil once fall soil cools below ~60F.

traits: Plant in fall — needs winter chill
Rot risk in soggy soil — keep drainage open
Buy disease-free seed garlic (not grocery store)
plants.tip: Plant cloves mid-October to early November so they root before winter; they need our winter chill to form bulbs. Your raised beds keep them out of soggy winter soil, the main cause of rot here. Side-dress with nitrogen in March as growth resumes. Hardnecks do well on the plateau: snap off the curly scapes in June (pesto!) so the plant puts energy into the bulb. Stop watering in late June, then dig in July when the bottom 2-3 leaves brown and cure 2-3 weeks in a dry, airy spot out of sun. Rotate: don't follow any allium.

plants.name: Shallots
plants.variety: Dutch Yellow / Dutch Red (fall-hardy); French hybrid Ambition or Pikant

care.label: Start method
care.value: Plant sets/cloves — fall or early spring

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: plant sets Oct-Nov (fall, like garlic) or Feb-Mar (spring); top of bulb 1 in below surface, point up

care.label: Harvest
care.value: Jul-Aug (when tops brown and fall over)

care.label: Water
care.value: Even moisture while growing (drip 2x/wk in dry spells); STOP watering as bulbs mature and pull back mulch so bulbs sit on the surface and dry down.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat — shallots go in as sets (small bulbs) either in fall with the garlic or as soon as the soil is workable in Feb-Mar.

traits: Each bulb makes a cluster of 6-10
Stop watering as bulbs size up
Keep weeded — shallow roots hate competition
plants.tip: Puget Sound allows both windows: plant with the garlic in Oct-Nov for the biggest bulbs (they need the winter chill), or in Feb-Mar if you miss fall. Each set splits into a cluster of 6-10 shallots, so space them generously. Full sun = fatter bulbs. Keep the soil weed-free, stop watering as tops flop, lift when most tops have browned (Jul-Aug), then cure 2-3 weeks with tops attached before trimming to 1 in and storing cool and dry. Early finish means they're out before the ridgegourd vines fill the space.

plants.name: Peas

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 2 in apart, rows 3-4 in along trellis

care.label: Water
care.value: Keep evenly moist spring through harvest; drip 1 in/wk, more during dry Jul-Aug for fall crop establishment.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat; peas are direct-sown outdoors and germinate fine in cool 45-55F soil.

plants.tip: Spring peas want cool soil, not cold mud: sow late February-March into the raised bed, which drains and warms faster than the ground, and net the row, since birds strip emerging sprouts in the backyard. They finish by late June, ahead of summer heat and mildew. For a fall crop, sow in early-mid July; later sowings run into October cold and mildew before they pod.

plants.name: Pole beans

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: early to mid Jun, once soil is above 60F

care.label: Water
care.value: Consistent moisture once flowering/podding; drip 2-3x/week through dry Jul-Aug, ease off as fall rains return.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No heat mat needed; pole beans are direct-sown, and seeds rot in cold soil regardless of indoor starting, so just wait for warm ground.

plants.tip: Don't sow until soil is reliably above 60F (early-mid June here) or seeds rot; protect emerging seedlings from slugs with bait or copper, as one wet night can wipe a whole row.

plants.name: Cabbage

care.label: Sow indoors
care.value: early-mid Jun (fall crop); Feb-early Mar (optional spring crop)

care.label: Harvest
care.value: late Sep-Nov (fall crop); holds in field through light frosts

care.label: Water
care.value: Consistent 1-1.5 in/week via drip all season; steady moisture prevents splitting. Dry Jul-Aug needs reliable irrigation; ease off as fall rains start.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Use the heat mat briefly to hit 75-80F for fast, even germination, then remove it once sprouted so seedlings stay stocky in cool light.

plants.tip: Cover with fine insect netting from transplant day onward; this is the single most effective control for cabbage worms/loopers and slugs, which are relentless on brassicas in the shaded maritime backyard.

plants.name: Cauliflower
plants.variety: Snow Crown (F1, ~50-60 days from transplant, reliable and relatively heat-forgiving for a cauliflower)

care.label: Sow indoors
care.value: late Jun to mid Jul (fall crop); optional early Mar for a spring crop

care.label: Plant out
care.value: late Jul to early Aug (fall); mid-late Apr (spring)

care.label: Harvest
care.value: late Sep to Nov (fall crop); partial shade adds ~1-2 wks

care.label: Water
care.value: Constant even moisture is critical; 1-1.5 in/wk on drip, more in dry Jul-Aug. Any check in moisture causes buttoning or ricey heads.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Use the heat mat to hit 70-75F for fast, even germination, then move seedlings off it immediately to cool, bright conditions so they don't stretch.

traits: Cabbage worm magnet (use floating row cover)
May need blanching for white heads
plants.tip: Grow it as a fall crop timed to mature in the cooling weather of Oct-Nov: heads set in cool, moist conditions, while summer-maturing heads button or go ricey. Keep under row cover from transplant to block cabbage worms.

plants.name: Tomato
plants.variety: 'Sungold' (early indeterminate cherry, reliably ripens), 'Stupice' (cold-tolerant, ~55 days), 'Oregon Spring' or 'Legend' (early determinate slicers; Legend has late-blight resistance)

care.label: Sow indoors
care.value: Late March to mid-April (about 6-8 weeks before transplant)

care.label: Plant out
care.value: Late May to early June, once nights stay above 50F (mid-May only inside a wall-o-water). Sammamish nights rarely stay above 55F before July, so early flowers set slowly; that is normal here. Black plastic or a wall-o-water banks soil heat.

care.label: Harvest
care.value: Late July through October (cherries first; bring green fruit indoors before cold/blight in Oct)

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 55-72 days from transplant (pick early/short-season types; in our cool summers anything over ~72 days rarely ripens before fall rain/blight)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: 18-24 in apart in-row, 36 in between rows; cherries/indeterminates need the wider end

care.label: Water
care.value: Water deeply and consistently at the soil line (never overhead) 1+ in/week through the dry July-August stretch to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking; water early in the day and keep foliage dry to slow late blight.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Tomato seed germinates fast and evenly only in warm soil (70-85F, ideally 75-85F); on a cool indoor windowsill germination stalls below 65F and seed can rot, so the heat mat is the single biggest difference-maker for strong, even starts. Pull seedlings off the mat once sprouted.

plants.tip: In our cool summers, variety choice is make-or-break: stick to early/short-season cherry and determinate types (Sungold, Stupice, Oregon Spring, Legend) that ripen in ~72 days or less, and give them the hottest full-sun front-yard spot with black plastic mulch or a wall-o-water. Nights stay under 55F until about July here, so early flowers may drop; don't plant out before late May unless inside a wall-o-water. Sungold and other cherries are indeterminate and need 6-ft+ stakes/cages; even determinate slicers should be staked. Late blight is the big killer in our wet Septembers and Octobers, so water only at the soil line early in the day, prune for airflow, keep foliage off the ground, and pick remaining fruit before the October rains set in.

plants.name: Fenugreek
plants.variety: Common methi (Trigonella foenum-graecum) bulk seed sown thickly for saag; Kasuri methi for a finer, more aromatic small-leaf type. Plain culinary/spice fenugreek seed from West Coast Seeds or Territorial works fine and is far cheaper than packet quantities.

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: Mid-Apr through mid-Sep; succession sow a fresh patch every 2-3 weeks. First sowing germinates slowly in cold maritime soil (50-55F), so the first reliable flush is late Apr-May. Spring (Apr-May) and fall (late Aug-Sep) sowings give the mildest, slowest-bolting leaves; skip mid-summer sowings or expect fast bolting and bitter foliage.

care.label: Harvest
care.value: May through October (peak in spring and again in fall)

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: 25-40 days from sowing to first leaf cut (~25 in warm spells, 35-40 in cool spring)

care.label: Spacing
care.value: Broadcast or sow ~1/2-1 in apart in bands; thin to 2-4 in for leafy clumps, rows 4-6 in apart. For saag, grow it thick like a baby-green carpet.

care.label: Water
care.value: Keep the seedbed evenly moist for fast germination and tender leaves; it needs steady water through the dry July-August stretch or it bolts and toughens early.

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: No mat needed: fenugreek is a cool-tolerant legume that germinates at 50-65F soil and is direct-sown anyway, so the heat mat brings no real advantage.

plants.tip: Direct sow only and never transplant: the taproot resents disturbance, so scatter seed thickly right in the partial-shade backyard alongside spinach, coriander, and arugula. Fast and easy (leaves in ~4-5 weeks) and cool-tolerant into the 40sF and through light frost, but cold maritime soil germinates it slowly, so the first April sowing is your slowest. Bolts quickly and turns bitter in the hot, dry July-August heat, so favor spring and late-summer/fall sowings and keep succession-sowing every 2-3 weeks. The biggest threat here is slugs mowing down the tender seedlings overnight, so bait or trap from the day you sow.

plants.name: Amaranth
plants.variety: Leafy vegetable amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor), green or red-leaf types; cultivar not specified

care.label: Sow indoors
care.value: early to mid May, about 4-5 weeks before June planting

care.label: Plant out
care.value: early to mid Jun after hardening off; soil at least 65F and nights consistently above 50F

care.label: Direct sow
care.value: Jun through late Jul once soil is warm; cover tiny seeds only 1/8-1/4 in deep and succession sow every 2-3 weeks

care.label: Harvest
care.value: Jul-Sep; early Oct only while weather stays mild, before frost

care.label: Time to harvest
care.value: ~30 days from transplant or 40-50 days from direct sowing; slower in cool weather

care.label: Spacing
care.value: Thin to 6 in apart for leafy harvests, rows 12-18 in apart; keep a sunny strip clear of vines and sunflower shade

care.label: Water
care.value: Keep the shallow seedbed evenly moist until emergence. Water at soil level through dry summer spells; drought brings earlier flowering and fewer tender leaves, but avoid waterlogging.

care.label: Germination
care.value: 70-80F ideal; wait for outdoor soil at least 65F, preferably near 70F

care.label: Heat mat
care.value: Optional for indoor starts: aim for 75-80F soil if the room is cool, then remove bottom heat after emergence. No mat needed for direct sowing into warm soil.

plants.tip: A summer green for the sunny front yard, outside the shade of the arches and sunflowers. Don't follow the spring spinach schedule: Sammamish soil isn't 65F until June, so start it indoors in May or direct sow in June-July. Pick tender leaves and shoot tips, leaving lower leaves to regrow, and pinch flower spikes to keep leaves coming and prevent self-seeding. Cold October nights end it, usually before frost.

plants.name: Rhododendron

care.label: Water
care.value: Even moisture; deep-water in summer dry spells (shallow roots); mulch 2–3 in

care.label: Prune
care.value: Right after bloom (May–Jun); deadhead spent trusses

care.label: Feed
care.value: Light, after bloom, with acid (rhododendron) fertilizer; stop by mid-July

plants.tip: Plateau soil is often gravelly glacial till over a hardpan that stays wet in winter, so plant at or slightly above grade, never deep, and mulch 2-3 in. Water deeply through our dry July-September; the shallow roots dry out fast. Notched leaf edges mean root weevils. Deadhead spent trusses by snapping them off above the new buds.

plants.name: Azalea

care.label: Feed
care.value: After bloom, acid fertilizer; stop by mid-July

plants.tip: Same care as rhododendron: plant high in the plateau's slow-draining till, mulch, and water through the dry summer. Stippled, bleached leaves with dark specks underneath mean azalea lace bug, worst in hot sun. Prune lightly right after flowering, before it sets next year's buds. Deciduous types add fall color.

plants.name: Camellia

care.label: Water
care.value: Even moisture; mulch. Buds set in summer — water through the dry summer or buds drop next spring

care.label: Feed
care.value: After bloom, acid (ericaceous) fertilizer — stop by the end of July to avoid bud drop

plants.tip: Two types extend the season — japonica blooms late winter to spring, sasanqua blooms in fall. Rake up and bin fallen flowers (don't compost) to prevent petal blight. Keep it watered through our dry summers, when next year's buds form, or buds drop the following spring.

plants.name: Hydrangea

care.label: Soil / pH
care.value: Rich, moist; bigleaf color shifts with pH (acidic = blue)

care.label: Water
care.value: Thirsty — deep-water in summer; wilts midday in heat

care.label: Prune
care.value: Bigleaf (mophead/lacecap): leave dead flower heads on over winter; in Apr-May, once hard frosts are past, cut each back to the first pair of fat buds. Panicle/smooth: late winter (new wood).

traits: Blooms on old vs new wood
plants.tip: Bigleaf (mophead/lacecap) hydrangeas flower on last year's stems. Leave the dead flower heads on over winter to shield the buds from our cold snaps, then in April-May, once hard frosts are past, cut each one back to the first pair of fat buds. Skip hard pruning, or you cut off the summer's flowers. Panicle and Annabelle types bloom on new wood, so prune those in late winter. Acidic soil turns bigleaf flowers blue. Water deeply through our dry July-September; they wilt fast.

plants.name: Hosta

care.label: Prune
care.value: Cut back dead foliage in late fall; divide spring or fall

traits: SLUG MAGNET — use the slug strategy
plants.tip: Slugs love hosta — start Sluggo at the very first spring shoots (the same slug strategy you use on the vegetables). It dies back fully in winter and returns in spring. Divide clumps in spring or fall to make more.

plants.name: Roses

care.label: Water
care.value: Deep, at the base — not overhead

care.label: Prune
care.value: Main prune late winter (Feb–Mar); deadhead through the season

care.label: Feed
care.value: Spring + early summer (stop by late Aug)

traits: Blackspot & powdery mildew in damp PNW
plants.tip: Our damp climate brings blackspot and powdery mildew pressure. Give full sun and air circulation, water at the base (not the leaves), clean up fallen leaves, and deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming. Main prune in late winter.

plants.name: Peony

care.label: Soil / pH
care.value: Rich, well-drained, near-neutral to slightly alkaline (lime acidic PNW soil)

care.label: Prune
care.value: Cut stems to the ground in fall

traits: Don't plant eyes too deep (1–2 in max)
plants.tip: Plant the buds ("eyes") only 1–2 inches deep — planting too deep is the classic reason peonies never bloom. Support the heavy flowers with a peony ring. Cut the foliage to the ground in fall to prevent botrytis. Ants on the buds are harmless. Don't move it once it's settled.

plants.name: Shasta daisy

care.label: Prune
care.value: Deadhead; cut back in fall; divide every 2–3 yrs

plants.tip: Deadhead spent flowers for more blooms. Tall types flop, so give support or grow compact varieties. Divide every 2–3 years to keep the clump vigorous.

plants.name: Hollyhock

care.label: Prune
care.value: Cut spent spikes; let some self-seed

plants.tip: Hollyhock rust is common in our damp climate — space plants for airflow, water at the base, and strip infected lower leaves. Clear away old foliage in fall (rust overwinters in debris). Stake only in windy, exposed spots. It self-seeds, so expect volunteers. Often blooms in its second year from seed.

plants.name: Tulips

care.label: Prune
care.value: Deadhead after bloom; let foliage die back naturally

care.label: Feed
care.value: Bulb food at planting; light feed in early spring as shoots emerge

traits: Rots in soggy winter soil — needs sharp drainage
plants.tip: Plant bulbs in October–November, 6–8 inches deep, in the sharpest-draining, sunniest spot. Hybrid tulips rarely rebloom well after their first spring, so many gardeners treat them as annuals or replant fresh bulbs each fall. The real risk here is wet, cold winter soil rotting the bulbs — our dry summers are ideal for their dormancy. Species/botanical tulips perennialize more reliably. Let the foliage yellow before removing it.

plants.name: Hyacinth

care.label: Feed
care.value: At planting, plus a feed as shoots emerge in spring

traits: First-year spike loosens later (replace every 2–3 yrs)
plants.tip: Plant in October-November, 4-6 inches deep, in the sunniest, best-drained spot: wet winter soil is what rots bulbs here, while our dry summers suit their dormancy. Blooms March-April and is intensely fragrant. The big first-year spike gets smaller and looser over time, so replace bulbs every few years for the best show. Wear gloves; the bulbs can irritate skin.

plants.name: Blueberry

care.label: Water
care.value: Consistent, especially while fruiting; shallow roots — mulch

care.label: Size
care.value: 5–8 ft (highbush; ~4–7 ft if pruned). Half-high types ~3–4 ft

care.label: Prune
care.value: Late winter, from year 3 — remove old/weak canes

traits: Self-fertile; 2+ varieties boost yield & berry size
plants.tip: The PNW is prime blueberry country. Give very acidic soil; blueberries are self-fertile, but planting two or more varieties (early + mid + late) gives bigger, earlier crops and a longer harvest — roughly mid-July into September. Net the bushes from birds. Mulch to protect the shallow roots; prune lightly in late winter from about year 3.

plants.name: Japanese barberry
plants.sun: Full sun (best color) to part shade

care.label: Sun
care.value: Full sun (best color) to part shade

care.label: Bloom
care.value: Minor yellow flowers Apr; grown for red/gold foliage

care.label: Prune
care.value: Anytime; shears well as a hedge (wear gloves — thorns)

plants.tip: Extremely low-maintenance — tough, drought-tolerant, and thorny (makes a good barrier hedge). Note it's considered invasive in parts of the US (banned in some eastern states; not in Washington) because birds spread the berries — choose a low-seed / near-sterile cultivar (none is fully sterile) and remove berries if that's a concern. Best foliage color in full sun.
